lead: An optical fiber communication system carries information as light. A transmitter turns an electrical signal into light, a glass fiber guides that light over distance, and a receiver turns it back into an electrical signal. Fiber is used because light in silica glass travels tens of kilometres with little loss, and because one fiber can carry many high-speed channels at once. Internet backbones, undersea cables, mobile tower links, cable TV and the fiber that reaches homes all use it.

sections.h3: The blocks of a fiber link

blocks.text: Every fiber link has three parts: a transmitter, the fiber channel and a receiver. The transmitter takes the electrical input, such as a bit stream from a router or an analog video signal, and a drive circuit turns it into a current that drives an optical source. The source is a light-emitting diode (LED) or a semiconductor laser, and the light power it emits follows the drive current.

The fiber is a thin strand of silica glass. Its central core has a slightly higher refractive index than the cladding around it, and that small index step keeps the light inside the core by total internal reflection (see Ray theory: total internal reflection, acceptance angle). A plastic coating protects the glass; it carries no light. Long links join fiber lengths with splices and connectors, and very long links add optical amplifiers or regenerators along the route.

The receiver uses a photodetector, usually a PIN photodiode or an avalanche photodiode (APD), to turn the arriving light into a current. An amplifier raises that small current, and a decision or filter circuit reshapes it into the electrical output.

items: Drive circuit and optical source: electrical to optical (E/O) conversion.
Fiber cable with splices, connectors and, on long routes, amplifiers or regenerators.
Amplifier and signal processing, then the electrical output.

blocks.text: Copper cable carries the signal as an electric current. Fiber carries it as light in glass. That one change gives these advantages.

items: Wide bandwidth. The optical carrier near 1550 nm has a frequency of about 1.94 × 10¹⁴ Hz, so even a small fraction of it is a huge band; a single fiber carries tens of gigabits per second on one wavelength, and wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) puts many wavelengths on the same fiber. The usable rate on one channel is set by the source, detector and electronics, but the fiber itself is not the bottleneck. A copper pair loses more and more signal as frequency rises.

Low loss. Silica is very transparent in the near infrared, so a signal travels tens of kilometres before it needs amplification. Copper links at high data rates need repeaters every few kilometres. The loss numbers are in the chapter Attenuation in optical fibers.

Immunity to electromagnetic interference. Glass is a dielectric, not a conductor, so nearby power lines, lightning and traction motors induce no noise in it, and the fiber radiates nothing that could disturb other circuits.
Electrical isolation. No metal joins the two ends, so there are no ground loops and no path for surge currents between buildings.
Safety. A fiber carries no current and makes no spark, so it can run through fuel depots, refineries and chemical plants.

Small size and weight. The bare glass is 125 µm across, about the thickness of a hair, and 250 µm with its coating. A cable holding dozens of fibers is lighter and thinner than a copper cable of far lower capacity, which eases duct and tower loading.
Security. Light stays in the core and nothing radiates, so the signal cannot be picked up by a nearby antenna. Tapping a fiber needs physical access and adds loss that monitoring can detect.
Cheap, plentiful raw material. Silica comes from sand, while copper is a costly metal.

blocks.text: Fiber also has drawbacks an examiner may ask for: splicing and connectors need precision tools, the glass breaks if bent too tightly, and the ends need E/O and O/E converters.

sections.h3: Analog and digital links, windows and the decibel

blocks.text: In an analog link the light power follows the input waveform continuously; radio-over-fiber feeds and older cable TV networks work this way. In a digital link the source is switched between two light levels and the receiver decides, in each bit slot, whether the light was high or low. Almost all telephone and internet traffic is digital.

Links are named by their wavelength window. 850 nm serves short multimode links inside buildings with cheap sources. 1310 nm is where pulse spreading in standard single-mode fiber is smallest, so it suits short and medium single-mode links. 1550 nm is where silica loss is lowest, so long-haul links use it. Loss and dispersion values come with signal degradation in fibers.
Loss in a fiber is quoted in decibels per kilometre, and the total loss in dB grows in proportion to length:

blocks.where: α is the attenuation in dB/km and L is the fiber length in km.
P is the optical power in mW; 0 dBm means exactly 1 mW. Powers in dBm and losses in dB add and subtract: P<sub>out</sub>(dBm) = P<sub>in</sub>(dBm) − loss (dB).

examples.question: A 20 km link at 1550 nm uses fiber with attenuation 0.2 dB/km. The source launches 1 mW. Find the total fiber loss, and the power reaching the receiver in dBm and in mW.
steps: Total loss: α × L = 0.2 dB/km × 20 km = 4 dB.
Launch power in dBm: 10 log₁₀(1 mW / 1 mW) = 10 log₁₀(1) = 0 dBm.
Received power in dBm: 0 dBm − 4 dB = −4 dBm.
Back to milliwatts: P = 1 mW × 10<sup>−4/10</sup> = 1 mW × 0.398 = 0.398 mW.
Check: a 3 dB loss halves the power, and 4 dB is a little more than that, so 0.398 mW (a little under half of 1 mW) is sensible.
examples.answer: The fiber loss is 4 dB; the receiver gets −4 dBm, which is 0.398 mW.

traps: Loss in dB grows with length: 0.2 dB/km is not the total loss. Add and subtract dB values; never multiply powers written in dB.
dBm is an absolute power (referred to 1 mW); dB is a ratio. 4 dB of loss takes 0 dBm to −4 dBm, not to 0.4 dBm.
The source is the E/O converter and the photodetector is the O/E converter. Do not swap them in the block diagram.
1310 nm is the low-dispersion window and 1550 nm the low-loss window; students often swap the two reasons.
Fiber's immunity to interference comes from glass being a dielectric. It does not come from the light being 'shielded' by the cladding.

quiz.q: Name the blocks of a general optical fiber link in order.
quiz.a: Electrical input, drive circuit and optical source (LED or laser), fiber with splices and connectors, photodetector (PIN or APD), amplifier and signal processing, electrical output.

quiz.q: What does the photodetector do in a fiber link?
quiz.a: It converts the arriving light into an electrical current (O/E conversion), which the receiver then amplifies and reshapes.

quiz.q: Why does a fiber link pick up no interference from a nearby traction motor?
quiz.a: The fiber is glass, a dielectric with no conductor along the path, so the motor's changing magnetic and electric fields induce no current in it. The signal is light, which these fields do not disturb.

quiz.q: A 12 km fiber has attenuation 0.25 dB/km and the launched power is 2 mW. Find the total loss and the received power in dBm and in mW.
quiz.a: Loss = 0.25 × 12 = 3 dB. 2 mW = 10 log₁₀2 = 3.01 dBm. Received power = 3.01 − 3 = 0.01 dBm = 2 × 10<sup>−0.3</sup> = 1.00 mW (a 3 dB loss halves the power).

quiz.q: Give two reasons why 1550 nm is chosen for long-haul links and 850 nm for links inside a building.
quiz.a: 1550 nm has the lowest loss in silica, so spans are longest. 850 nm links are short, so loss matters less, and cheap LEDs and VCSELs with multimode fiber are available there.

quiz.q: A technician reads 0.4 mW at the end of a 20 km, 0.2 dB/km fiber fed with 1 mW. Is the reading consistent? Show the dB working.
quiz.a: Yes. Loss = 0.2 × 20 = 4 dB; 1 mW = 0 dBm; expected 0 − 4 = −4 dBm = 0.398 mW, which rounds to 0.4 mW. No extra connector or splice loss is needed to explain the reading.

quiz.q: A plant wants to link a control room to a pump house inside a petrol depot. Argue for fiber instead of copper using two advantages.
quiz.a: Fiber carries no current and makes no spark, so it is safe in a flammable area; and it gives electrical isolation, so a lightning strike or ground fault at the pump house cannot reach the control room through the cable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Coherent links send data on the amplitude and phase of one 1550 nm carrier and recover it with digital signal processing, so one wavelength carries hundreds of gigabits per second. Research systems use multi-core fiber, several cores in one cladding, to multiply capacity again. Silicon photonics puts modulators and detectors on a chip next to the fiber to cut cost in data centres. Search next for coherent optical transmission, multi-core fiber and silicon photonics transceivers.
